item.title: Garage Door Spam
item.description:
Source: blog.harrison.page

Top Comment:

The Chaimberlain / MyQ situation is terrible. I strongly recommend avoiding them all together.

I recently installed a Chaimberlain garage door opener in a location that required three buttons inside the garage. They limit the buttons in software, so that each garage door opener can have only two at any given time!

After some tinkering, I discovered that the Chaimberlain buttons transmit their signal wirelessly these days, even when "wired" to the garage door opener... the wires only provide power. So...

I worked around the problem by placing a dab of solder on one of their security+ 3.0 buttons so that it is always "pressed." Then I wired up the three old school garage door momentary switches to send power to it. When pressed, they power up the Chaimberlain button, which then sends a wireless signal to open the door.

item.title: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion
item.description:
Source: www.ruby-lang.org

Top Comment:

There's what I think is probably an awesome bug here.

Windows-1252 encoding has a representation for lowercase German sharp 's' (ß), but not one for the uppercase. If you upcase a string containing a sharp 's', it gets normalized to "SS", which increases the length of the string by one character. The 1252 case conversion code doesn't handle this; it looks like it checks for headroom in the buffer one character at a time. So if the last character of a string you upcase is ß, it looks like you get a one-byte overflow (of 'S').

If that's really the bug (there's a claimed RCE POC), the heap grooming for it must be really fussy! I couldn't find any other character pairs that expand like this.

You can feed strings in 1252 to a Rails program through multipart POSTs, which get to pick their encodings.

The great thing about this bug, apart from how it illustrates how doomed we all are (if I'm right), is that it should by rights have the best vulnerability name of the year, because you get to work 'ß' into it.

item.title: LLM assisted reverse engineering
item.description:
Source: www.slowchronicle.com

Top Comment:

Yesterday night, i reverse engineered the cloud connection plugin to my cctv camera in about 2 hours with Gemini.

Started off with me searching for what Chinese OEM made the product. Then tried out existing GitHub projects to see if it works but they were failing.

Spent 15 minutes to write a script that started their desktop software on a different network namespace and ran tcpdump in it. Captured exactly only the things i needed without any noise. Turned out it was using a different server url and credentials than the GitHub projects. Opened Ghidra to inspect the dlls that matched the strings i was looking for.

After that, I got lazy and handed over the task to Gemini to find the username and key they use to authenticate with the servers. It took about 30 minutes or an hour. A lot of it was me changing models because the llm servers were busy. It simply wrote a little script that ran through various strings it fetched from the binary to see if it can generate the authentication credentials.

Now my Home Assistant will be detecting if my car is parked in the parking lot or not. Life is good.

item.title: SSD prices may begin to decline in the latter half of 2027
item.description:
Source: www.drivevault.io

Top Comment:

If you look at valuation of a company like Micron (MU), it's pretty clear that the market expects a collapse in their profits. They are growing at absolutely insane rates, whether you look at YoY (well over +300%) or QoQ (over +40%) in both revenue and profits. Yet their PE is below 10. SK Hynix is similar.

A typical company that trades at a sub-10 PE is a flatline-to-dying business whose last juice is being squeezed out before the inevitable sale of remaining valuable assets and dissolution.

Of course the current market price is not a perfect predictor of the future of a business but despite all the memes and anecdotes, the market is far more often basically right than dramatically wrong (it's just that when it does get things dramatically wrong, that's what gets all the publicity, for obvious reasons).

So, assuming the market is roughly right in its valuation of Micron or SK Hynix, either demand will collapse or supply will surge or, some combo of the two. Either way it seems extremely likely that within a couple of years at most the prices of DRAM and NAND will come waaaay down.

item.title: UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order
item.description:
Source: macanorak.com

Top Comment:

Apple has significantly weakened its security assurances in a way that is arguably deceptive. They used to say nobody can access your data, not even Apple. Now they say Apple cannot access your data. People will point out that your key is created on your device, lives on your device, and never leaves your device, but that is just your key. Your key is likely a KEK (key encryption key) that opens another key (not “your” key, let’s call it the actual key) that your data is secured with. There can be other parties (UK government) with their own KEK that opens a copy of the actual key. In this scenario, Apple can have no access to a KEK that opens the actual key, but they are forced to make the wording change they did, if they want to stay honest.

I say the statement is arguably deceptive because it presents the same feel of assurance that the old one did, to most people.

Note John Ternus in a recent event (WWDC keynote if I recall correctly) used the old wording. I think this was a slip-up (I’d hate to think it was a calculated lie posing as a slip-up).
